prompt: Some people believe that schools should teach practical skills such as cooking, budgeting and basic repairs instead of concentrating on traditional academic subjects. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
outline: Partly agree: practical skills matter but should not replace academic subjects
Body 1: school leavers lack money and life skills, e.g. budgeting after the first salary
Body 2: academic subjects build reasoning and are hard to learn later; practical skills are quick to learn
Solution: short compulsory practical strand added to the timetable

band7.essay:
Some people argue that schools should spend more time teaching practical skills like cooking, managing money and simple repairs instead of traditional academic subjects. I partly agree with this view, because these skills are useful in daily life, but I do not think academic subjects should be replaced.

On the one hand, practical skills are very important for young people. Many students in Bangladesh finish school without knowing how to make a budget or compare prices, so they often struggle when they start living alone or earning a salary. For example, a graduate who has never learned about saving may spend most of his first salary in a few weeks. Cooking and basic repairs can also save families money and help students become more independent. Learning these things early also gives students confidence, because they feel ready for adult life.

On the other hand, academic subjects such as mathematics, science and languages build thinking skills that are needed for almost every career. Without a strong base in these subjects, students cannot go to university or become doctors, engineers or teachers. In addition, practical skills can often be learned at home or through short courses, while it is difficult to learn physics or advanced mathematics without a teacher. Therefore, schools are the best place for academic learning. For this reason, I believe that academic subjects must stay at the centre of the timetable.

In conclusion, I agree that schools should give more attention to practical skills, but this should be done by adding short lessons to the timetable, not by reducing the main academic subjects. A balance would prepare students for both exams and real life.
band7.comment: Clear position, relevant examples and logical paragraphs make this Band 7. It is held back by plain vocabulary (very important, useful), some repeated ideas and limited use of more precise collocations or complex structures.

band8.essay:
It is sometimes claimed that classrooms should make room for cooking, budgeting and basic repairs at the expense of traditional subjects. I agree that such skills deserve a place in the curriculum, but I disagree that they should displace academic study.

The case for practical education is strong. Many school leavers in Dhaka can solve a quadratic equation yet cannot read a loan agreement or work out the true cost of an instalment purchase. Financial literacy in particular protects young adults from debt traps, and a basic grasp of nutrition and cooking helps them eat well on a limited income. These abilities are rarely taught at home in any systematic way, so schools can fill a genuine gap. Schools in Bangladesh already run science fairs and debates, so a regular workshop on household budgeting would not be a radical departure.

However, replacing academic subjects would be shortsighted. Mathematics, science and language teach students to reason, test claims and communicate precisely, and these capacities transfer to nearly every profession, including those that do not yet exist. Moreover, a child who is denied a rigorous grounding at fifteen can rarely recover it later, whereas practical competence is acquired relatively quickly through a short course or an apprenticeship. A budgeting module takes weeks to learn; algebra takes years. Employers, too, tend to value graduates who can analyse a problem and write clearly more than those who hold a single narrow competence.

In short, practical skills are best introduced as a compact, compulsory strand alongside the existing curriculum, perhaps one afternoon a week, rather than as a substitute for it. This arrangement equips students to pass examinations and to manage adult life with confidence.
band8.comment: The position is nuanced and sustained throughout, ideas are developed with specific, contrasting examples, and vocabulary is precise (debt traps, rigorous grounding, practical competence). Cohesion is smooth and the closing proposal is concrete.

structure.note: States a partial-agreement position that answers the question directly.
Argues for practical skills using a concrete gap between academic ability and financial literacy.
Concedes the counter-view and shows why academic learning cannot be postponed.
Proposes a compact practical strand as a workable compromise.

vocab.m: ability to do useful real tasks
with a loss to something else

prompt: Some people say that governments should ban single-use plastic items such as bags and bottles, instead of asking people to reduce their use voluntarily. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
outline: Position: mostly agree, a ban works better than appeals
Voluntary schemes fail because convenience and low cost win
Bans change shop and factory behaviour at once, with examples like Bangladesh's jute bag law
Condition: affordable alternatives and enforcement are needed

band7.essay:
Plastic waste is a serious problem in many countries, and I largely agree that governments should ban single-use items rather than rely on voluntary action.

The main reason is that individual choices are rarely strong enough to change the situation. Most people know that plastic bags block drains and pollute rivers, but they still accept them because they are free and convenient. In Dhaka, for example, drainage systems regularly become blocked by plastic during the monsoon, and campaigns asking people to use cloth bags have had little lasting effect. A legal ban removes the choice, so the whole market has to change at the same time. Bangladesh was actually the first country to ban thin polythene bags in 2002, which shows that the idea is possible, even though the law has not always been enforced.

Another advantage of a ban is that it pushes businesses to develop alternatives. When shops and factories know that plastic products will no longer be sold, they begin to invest in paper, jute or biodegradable packaging. This creates new jobs and can even support local farmers who grow jute. If the government only asks for voluntary reduction, companies have no reason to spend money on change. However, a ban alone is not enough. Alternatives must be cheap enough for ordinary families and small street sellers, otherwise the rule will simply be ignored. Inspectors must also check markets regularly, or the law may exist only on paper.

In conclusion, I believe a ban is a more effective approach than voluntary reduction, provided that the government supports it with affordable substitutes and strict enforcement.
band7.comment: Clear position, relevant Bangladesh examples and logical paragraphing place this in Band 7. Vocabulary is accurate but fairly general, and some ideas, such as the effect on small sellers, are stated rather than developed in depth.

band8.essay:
I broadly agree that governments should prohibit single-use plastics outright, because appeals to personal responsibility have repeatedly failed to deliver results at the scale the problem demands.

The weakness of voluntary schemes lies in the gap between awareness and behaviour. Most shoppers understand that discarded polythene clogs drains and poisons waterways, yet when a free bag is offered at the counter, convenience prevails. Dhaka's monsoon flooding, aggravated by blocked drainage, illustrates how the cost of that small decision is borne collectively rather than by the individual making it. When the harm is shared but the benefit is private, exhortation rarely works, and regulation becomes the more logical tool.

A ban also reshapes supply, not just demand. Once a product is illegal, manufacturers and retailers must invest in substitutes, and the market for alternatives can grow quickly. Jute, a traditional crop in Bangladesh, is an obvious candidate, and a firm legal signal could turn a declining industry into a source of export income and rural employment. Voluntary schemes offer no such certainty, so companies hesitate to commit capital. That said, I would qualify my support. Bangladesh introduced a polythene ban as early as 2002, yet bags remain widespread, which demonstrates that legislation without enforcement is meaningless. Authorities must therefore inspect markets, penalise repeat offenders, and ensure that replacements are affordable for street vendors operating on thin margins. Otherwise, a ban may simply push people towards an informal trade in prohibited goods.

In sum, voluntary reduction is a useful complement but a poor foundation for policy. A well-enforced ban, paired with accessible alternatives, offers the only realistic means of changing behaviour across an entire society.
band8.comment: The essay takes a clear, qualified position and develops each point with cause and effect, such as the shared-harm argument and the supply-side effect. Vocabulary is precise and flexible, and the Bangladeshi example is used to support a counter-argument as well.

structure.note: Restates the issue and gives a clear, slightly qualified position in one sentence.
Explains why voluntary action fails, using the idea of shared harm and a local flooding example.
Shows how a ban reshapes supply (jute example), then qualifies support by stressing enforcement and affordability.
Summarises the conditions under which a ban succeeds and ranks voluntary action as secondary.

vocab.p: the gap between awareness and behaviour
vocab.m: knowing something but not acting on it
a helpful addition, not the main tool

prompt: Some people believe that working from home is better for both employees and employers than working in an office. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
outline: Position: mostly agree, with limits for some jobs
Employees: no commute, flexible time, better balance
Employers: lower rent and costs, wider hiring pool
Limit: teamwork and training suffer without contact

band7.essay:
In recent years, many companies have allowed staff to work remotely. I largely agree that this arrangement benefits both employees and employers, although it is not suitable for every job.

For employees, the main advantage is saving time and money. In a city like Dhaka, people may spend three hours a day stuck in traffic, which is tiring and expensive. When they work from home, they can use this time to rest, exercise or be with their family. Remote work also gives workers more control over their schedule, so they can organise their day around their energy levels, and this often leads to better concentration and less stress. Employers also gain a lot. A firm with fewer workers in the office needs a smaller building, and rent and electricity are among the biggest costs for a business. In addition, companies are not limited to people who live nearby, so they can hire talented staff from other cities or even other countries. Several studies show that satisfied employees are more productive, which means that the company profits as well.

However, I do not believe that working from home is perfect. New employees often learn faster when they sit near experienced colleagues and can ask questions immediately. Creative teams may also find it harder to share ideas through a screen. Moreover, in Bangladesh, power cuts and slow internet can interrupt work at home. For these reasons, a mixture of office days and home days may be the best solution for many organisations.

In conclusion, remote work saves time and money for workers and reduces costs for employers, so I mostly agree with the statement. Nevertheless, jobs that depend on teamwork, training or reliable equipment still need some office presence.
band7.comment: Clear position, relevant examples and mostly accurate grammar earn Band 7. Ideas are sensible but general, linking is fairly mechanical, and vocabulary such as 'a lot' and 'perfect' is not precise enough for a higher band.

band8.essay:
Remote work, once an exception, is now a mainstream option. I largely agree that it serves both employees and employers well, provided it is not treated as a universal replacement for the office.

The benefits for employees are tangible. In Dhaka, a daily commute can swallow three hours and a considerable share of a modest salary, and eliminating it returns that time to rest, study or family life. Workers also gain autonomy over their schedules, which allows them to tackle demanding tasks when they are most alert. Such flexibility is closely linked to lower burnout and higher job satisfaction, outcomes that employers should value. Employers stand to gain just as much. Office space and utilities are among the largest fixed costs of a business, and a partly remote workforce can cut both substantially. Furthermore, recruitment is no longer confined to those who can reach a particular building; a Chattogram software firm, for instance, can hire a skilled developer in Sylhet or abroad without relocation expenses. Because contented staff tend to stay longer, the company also saves on the cost of replacing them.

That said, the arrangement has genuine limits. Junior employees learn largely by observation, and the casual advice of a nearby colleague is hard to replicate on a video call. Collaborative work such as product design can also lose momentum when spontaneous conversation disappears. In countries where load-shedding and unstable broadband remain common, home working may even reduce reliability.

In short, working from home delivers real savings and freedom for both sides, which is why I broadly agree with the statement. The most sensible model, however, is a hybrid one in which remote days handle focused work and office days are reserved for mentoring and teamwork.
band8.comment: Precise collocations (autonomy, fixed costs, confined to, spontaneous conversation) and concrete local examples are woven into a tightly argued response. Each paragraph has one controlling idea, concessions are balanced, and cohesion comes from meaning rather than formulaic linkers.

structure.note: Paraphrases the topic and states a clear, qualified position (largely agree).
Develops employee benefits (commute, autonomy, burnout) and employer gains (costs, wider hiring).
Concedes genuine limits in training, collaboration and infrastructure, supporting a hybrid model.
Restates the position and proposes a hybrid model as the practical answer.

vocab.m: use up a lot of time
freedom to control their own time
expenses that stay the same regardless of output
limited to a particular place or group
mix of home and office work

prompt: Some people believe that voting in national elections should be compulsory for all adult citizens. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
outline: Position: mostly agree, with sensible exceptions
Representative results and politicians listening to all groups
Counter-view: personal freedom and uninformed votes
Safeguards: blank ballot option, fair penalties

band7.essay:
Some people argue that every adult should be required to vote in national elections. I agree with this idea to a large extent, because it can make democracy stronger, although there are some practical problems that need to be considered.

The main reason for supporting compulsory voting is that it produces results which represent the whole population. In many countries, including Bangladesh, turnout in some elections is low, so the winners are chosen by only a small part of society. If everyone had to vote, politicians would need to listen to all citizens, including poor and rural people whom they often ignore. Compulsory voting can also encourage people to learn about the parties and their plans, since they know that they must make a decision on election day.

However, there are some disadvantages to this system. Forcing people to vote is a limit on personal freedom, and some citizens may feel angry about it. Others may vote without any interest and simply choose a name at random, which does not really help democracy. In addition, the government would have to fine people who do not vote, and this could be unfair to those who are ill or who live far away from polling stations, such as people in remote char areas.

Despite these problems, I believe the benefits are greater. The difficulties can be reduced if voters are allowed to leave their ballot blank and if there are clear exceptions for illness or travel. In conclusion, compulsory voting can make elections fairer and more representative, as long as the system is organised carefully and the penalties are reasonable.
band7.comment: Clear position, relevant ideas and good organisation. Vocabulary and linking are mostly accurate but fairly basic, and the ideas are not developed as deeply or precisely as in a higher band.

band8.essay:
Whether the state should oblige adults to vote is a question on which I lean towards agreement, provided the obligation is accompanied by sensible safeguards.

The strongest argument in favour is legitimacy. When turnout is low, governments are elected by a self-selecting minority, and policy tends to reflect the priorities of those who habitually vote: the urban, the educated and the organised. Compulsory attendance changes the incentives of politicians, who can no longer win by mobilising a loyal base alone and must address groups they would otherwise neglect, such as garment workers or farmers in remote districts. Australia, where voting is mandatory, offers a useful illustration, since its parties compete for the political centre rather than relying on extreme supporters. Furthermore, the habit of voting may nurture civic awareness, as people who must choose are more likely to follow public debate.

Critics object that compulsion infringes individual liberty and produces careless ballots. There is some truth in this, but the objection is weaker than it first appears. The duty is to attend, not to endorse a candidate, so allowing a blank or "none of the above" option preserves freedom of conscience. Random voting, meanwhile, is a marginal problem compared with the distortion caused by mass abstention. A more serious concern is fairness: a fine would punish the sick, migrant workers and those who live far from a polling station. This can be addressed through postal or mobile voting, generous exemptions and modest penalties.

In conclusion, I agree that voting should be compulsory, because broad participation gives governments a stronger mandate and forces them to serve the whole population. The policy is defensible only if it is administered flexibly and fairly.
band8.comment: Position is stated precisely and sustained. The essay uses a concrete comparison, anticipates and answers the opposing argument, and shows wide, natural vocabulary with accurate complex sentences.

structure.note: Gives a clear position with a qualification (agree, with safeguards).
Develops the main argument: legitimacy, changed incentives for politicians, and a concrete example.
Rebuts the freedom objection and deals with fairness through practical solutions.
Restates the position and ties it to the condition of fair administration.

vocab.m: a small group that chooses itself
right to follow one's own beliefs

prompt: Smartphones should be banned from classrooms in all schools. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
outline: Mostly agree: phones are a major distraction
Body 1: distraction, poorer listening and results, less face-to-face talk
Body 2: counter-view (dictionary, safety) can be met by other means
Allow limited use only with teacher permission

band7.essay:
Mobile phones are now common among school students, and some people think they should be completely banned in classrooms. I agree with this opinion to a large extent, because phones usually distract students, although there are a few situations where they can help.

The main reason for a ban is distraction. Students who have a phone on their desk often check messages, social media or games during lessons, so they miss important explanations. In many schools in Bangladesh, teachers already complain that students do not listen carefully and their results become worse. A ban would remove this problem, and students would also talk to each other more during breaks instead of looking at screens. Some students even use their phones to cheat in exams, which is unfair to honest students and damages the reputation of the school.

However, some people say that phones can be useful learning tools. Students can look up words in an online dictionary or watch a short video to understand a difficult topic. Also, parents may want their children to carry a phone for safety when they travel to school alone. These points are reasonable, but I think they do not need phones to be used inside the classroom. Schools can provide computers for research, and students can keep their phones in their bags during lessons so that parents can still contact them after school. Teachers can also use projectors and printed handouts to show videos or pictures, so phones are not really needed.

In conclusion, I mostly agree that phones should be banned in classrooms because the distraction is greater than the benefits. Schools should allow limited use only when a teacher gives permission for a specific activity.
band7.comment: The essay answers the question with a clear opinion and sensible support, so it reaches Band 7. It stays at this level because the ideas are fairly general, there is little precise vocabulary, and the counter-argument is handled quickly.

band8.essay:
Smartphones have become so common among teenagers that many schools now struggle to hold their attention. I largely agree that they should be barred from classrooms, with narrow exceptions for teacher-led use.

The strongest argument for a ban is that phones undermine concentration even when they are not being used. Studies of attention suggest that a phone lying face down on a desk still draws on a student's mental effort, since part of the mind stays alert for notifications. In a crowded classroom of fifty pupils, which is not unusual in Bangladesh, a single buzzing device can derail a lesson for everyone. Schools in several countries that have introduced bans report calmer corridors, more conversation at break time and, in some cases, modest gains in test scores. Teachers also lose precious minutes policing devices, which turns the classroom into a contest of wills rather than a place of shared inquiry.

Opponents point out that phones can serve as dictionaries, cameras and research tools, and that parents value being able to reach their children. These benefits are real but can be secured by other means. A school can supply shared tablets or a computer lab for supervised research, and families can contact the office in an emergency. Where a teacher wants students to scan a diagram or check a definition, supervised use can be allowed for that task and the devices collected again, which retains the advantage without the constant temptation. Parents can reasonably expect to be reached through the school office, as they were before mobile phones existed.

Overall, the costs of unrestricted phone access in class outweigh its educational value. A firm default ban, softened by controlled exceptions, would let teachers teach and students learn.
band8.comment: The writer commits to a precise position (a default ban with exceptions) and anticipates objections with practical alternatives. Vocabulary such as undermine concentration, derail a lesson and controlled exceptions is natural, and the paragraphs are tightly organised.

structure.note: Gives a qualified position that signals the exact scope of the ban.
Explains distraction even from unused phones and links it to large Bangladeshi classes.
Answers the usefulness and safety objections with practical alternatives.
Restates the weighing of costs against benefits in one balanced sentence.

prompt: Some people think that the best way to improve public health is to make healthy food cheaper than unhealthy food, rather than to educate people about diet. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
outline: Position: agree that price matters more than education alone
Poor families buy what they can afford, even when they know better
Subsidies for vegetables, fruit and fish versus taxes on sugary drinks
Education still has a supporting role

band7.essay:
Many people now suffer from diabetes, heart disease and obesity, and governments are looking for ways to improve diets. In my opinion, making healthy food cheaper is a more effective solution than education alone, although both are useful.

First, price strongly affects what families buy, especially in low-income households. In Bangladesh, many workers spend most of their income on food, so they often choose rice, oil and cheap snacks because these fill them up at low cost. Fresh fish, fruit and vegetables can be expensive in the city, even if people know they are good for health. Telling these families to eat better does not help if they cannot afford it. When the government lowers the price of healthy items, for example by supporting farmers or controlling market prices, people can actually follow the advice they receive.

Second, cheaper healthy food can change habits for a whole population, not just for people who attend a health class. A tax on sugary drinks, together with lower prices on vegetables, would make the healthy option the easy option. Several countries have introduced soda taxes, and sales of these drinks have fallen. This kind of policy reaches everyone, including people who never read health information. On the other hand, education should not be ignored. Some people simply do not know that too much sugar or fried food is harmful, and children need to learn good habits at school. Cheap vegetables will not be bought if people do not know how to cook them or why they matter.

In conclusion, I agree that lowering the cost of healthy food has a stronger effect than education, but the best result will come when the two approaches are combined.
band7.comment: The position is clear and ideas are relevant and sensibly organised, which supports Band 7. The language is accurate but repetitive in places, and the claim about soda taxes is not supported with specific evidence.

band8.essay:
I largely agree that lowering the price of nutritious food would do more for public health than education campaigns, although I do not think the latter should be abandoned.

The central difficulty is that knowledge is not the main barrier to healthy eating for most low-income families. A garment worker in Dhaka may well know that vegetables and fish are better than fried snacks and refined rice, but when food consumes a large share of a modest wage, calories per taka become the deciding factor. Advice that ignores this reality is not merely ineffective; it can feel patronising. By contrast, price signals work on everyone regardless of literacy or interest, so a subsidy on seasonal produce or a levy on sugary drinks shifts behaviour at the population level.

Evidence from other countries supports this view. Several cities that introduced taxes on sweetened beverages recorded a measurable fall in sales, and the revenue was often directed towards health programmes. Making the healthy choice the cheaper choice removes the need for constant willpower, which is precisely what busy people lack. Nevertheless, education retains an important supporting role. Some people genuinely underestimate the dangers of excess sugar and oil, and children who learn basic nutrition at school may carry that understanding into adulthood. Cheaper ingredients are also of limited value if households lack the skills to prepare them in appealing ways.

To conclude, affordability is the stronger lever because it addresses the practical constraint that most often determines what ends up on the plate. Education should follow as a complement, ensuring that people make the best use of the options that policy has made accessible.
band8.comment: The argument is built around one strong central idea, that knowledge is not the main barrier, and each paragraph advances it with reasoning rather than listing points. Collocations such as 'price signals' and 'population level' are natural, and the concession paragraph is balanced without weakening the position.

structure.note: States agreement with a built-in concession so the position is nuanced from the start.
Argues that cost, not knowledge, is the real barrier, using a garment worker example.
Backs the price argument with international evidence on sugar taxes, then concedes education still has a supporting role.
Calls affordability the stronger lever and places education as a follow-up.

vocab.m: how much food energy money buys
a special tax on such drinks
still helps, but is not the main tool
the more effective way to cause change

prompt: Some people think that parents, rather than schools, should be responsible for teaching children good behaviour and moral values. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
outline: Position: mostly agree, schools support
Home is where values are first learned by example
Parents know child best, time and emotional bond
Schools reinforce through rules and peers

band7.essay:
Many people argue that children should learn good behaviour and values at home rather than in school. I agree with this view to a large extent, but I think teachers also have a supporting role.

The main reason is that children learn first from their families. From a very young age, they copy the way their parents speak, treat elders and handle anger. For example, a child who sees his father respecting neighbours and helping people in need will probably do the same. Parents also spend much more time with children than teachers do, so they have more chances to correct mistakes and give advice. This close emotional bond makes children more willing to listen. In addition, parents know their own children's character better than anyone else. A teacher may have forty students in a class in Bangladesh and cannot give each of them personal attention. If a child lies or is rude to others, a parent can talk to him privately and explain why this is wrong, which is more effective than a general lesson.

On the other hand, schools cannot be ignored. Children spend about six hours a day in school, and they meet students from different backgrounds there. Teachers can set rules about honesty, punctuality and respect, and they can punish bullying. Some parents are also busy working long hours, so schools may need to fill the gap.

In conclusion, I agree that moral education is mainly the duty of parents because they are the first role models and know their children well. However, schools should reinforce these values so that children receive the same message in both places.
band7.comment: The response is relevant, organised and develops each point with an example, which fits Band 7. Some ideas are repeated ('more time', 'know better'), the examples are generic, and there are minor imprecisions in word choice.

band8.essay:
Whether character is formed at home or in the classroom is a long-standing debate. I largely agree that parents carry the primary responsibility for instilling values, although schools have an important reinforcing role.

Children absorb moral habits long before they enter a classroom. They imitate how adults speak to servants, argue with relatives or react to unfairness, and these early impressions tend to be remarkably durable. A boy who watches his mother return extra change to a shopkeeper learns honesty more convincingly than from any lecture. Moreover, the emotional trust between parent and child gives guidance a weight that a teacher's instruction rarely has. Practical considerations reinforce this argument as well. A teacher in a typical Bangladeshi school may be responsible for forty or more pupils and, realistically, cannot tailor advice to each one's temperament. Parents, by contrast, notice subtle changes, such as a child who begins to lie or withdraw, and can respond at once and in private, which avoids public embarrassment.

Nevertheless, it would be unwise to absolve schools entirely. Pupils spend much of their waking day there, and the playground tests values such as fairness and cooperation in ways that home cannot. Clear rules against bullying and cheating also signal that standards apply beyond the family. This is especially valuable, and sometimes essential, when parents work long hours or are absent, for example because they are employed overseas, as many Bangladeshi parents are.

In conclusion, parents should lead moral education because they are the earliest and most influential models, whereas schools are best placed to consolidate those lessons. The most positive outcomes occur when both deliver a consistent message.
band8.comment: Ideas are developed with specific, believable illustrations and a controlled concession paragraph. Vocabulary is accurate and flexible (instilling, durable, absolve, consolidate) and complex sentences are used without loss of clarity.

structure.note: Frames the debate and gives a clear position that parents lead and schools support.
Argues that early imitation, emotional trust and class-size limits make parents the main influence.
Concedes the school's role through peer testing, anti-bullying rules and gaps left by absent parents.
Summarises the division of responsibility and stresses consistency between home and school.

prompt: Some people think that the most effective way to reduce crime is to introduce much harsher punishments. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
outline: Position: disagree that harsher punishment is the most effective
Certainty of being caught deters more than severity
Root causes: poverty, unemployment, weak education
Some serious crimes still need firm sentences

band7.essay:
It is sometimes said that stricter punishments are the best way to bring down crime. I partly disagree with this view, because I think other measures are more effective in the long term, although tough penalties do have a role for serious offences.

Those who support harsh punishment believe that fear of a long prison sentence will stop people from breaking the law. This is true in some cases. For example, when a country introduces very heavy penalties for drug smuggling, some criminals may decide that the risk is too high. Serious violent crimes also need strong sentences so that dangerous people cannot harm others and victims feel that justice has been done.

On the other hand, I do not believe that severe punishment alone can solve the problem. Many criminals do not think about the punishment when they commit a crime, because they expect that they will not be caught. In my opinion, a higher chance of being arrested is a stronger deterrent than a longer sentence, so governments should invest in police, street lighting and faster courts. In addition, crime is often caused by poverty and unemployment. A young man with no job and no education may join a gang simply to earn money. If the government provides training and job opportunities, fewer people will turn to crime in the first place.

To conclude, harsher punishments can discourage some serious crimes, but they are not the most effective solution. A combination of effective policing, education and employment is likely to reduce crime more successfully than severe penalties alone.
band7.comment: Position is clear and the essay answers the question with relevant examples. Some ideas are general, a few phrases are repetitive, and the language lacks the range and precision needed for Band 8.

band8.essay:
I disagree that harsher punishment is the most effective way to cut crime. Severe penalties have a limited place, but evidence and common sense suggest that other measures work better and last longer.

The case for severity rests on deterrence: if the cost of crime rises, rational people will avoid it. This logic holds for a narrow range of offences that are planned in advance, such as smuggling or large-scale corruption, where offenders weigh risks carefully. Long sentences for violent offenders also serve a separate purpose, since they keep dangerous individuals away from the public and show victims that the law takes their suffering seriously.

Nevertheless, deterrence depends far less on the size of the penalty than on the likelihood of being caught. A snatcher in a crowded Dhaka market or a teenager committing an impulsive assault rarely calculates the sentence; he assumes he will escape. Where detection is unlikely, raising the punishment from five years to ten changes almost nothing. Resources are therefore better spent on visible policing, reliable investigation and courts that reach verdicts within months rather than years. Equally important are the conditions that produce offenders, because punishment arrives only after harm has been done. Persistent youth unemployment, poor schooling and weak community support make criminal gangs an attractive source of income and belonging. Vocational training and rehabilitation inside prisons reduce reoffending, whereas overcrowded jails often turn minor offenders into hardened ones, with little chance of finding honest work afterwards.

In conclusion, tougher sentences should be reserved for the gravest crimes, but they are not the primary solution. A justice system that catches offenders quickly and a society that offers young people real opportunities will do more to reduce crime than severity alone.
band8.comment: The essay concedes the valid point, then argues that certainty of detection matters more than severity, supported by realistic, specific examples. Vocabulary is precise and the argument is controlled from start to finish.

structure.note: States disagreement and acknowledges a limited role for severity.
Explains why detection and speed of justice matter more than sentence length.
Adds root causes and the negative effect of overcrowded prisons.
Summarises the position and the better combination of measures.

vocab.m: a thief who grabs things and runs
criminals made more dangerous by prison
used only for the worst crimes

prompt: Some people think that university education should be free for all students, while others believe that students should pay for it. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
outline: View 1: free tuition gives equal opportunity and benefits society
View 2: public money is limited; fees protect quality; graduates earn more
Opinion: low fees plus scholarships and loans

band7.essay:
Some people believe that governments should pay for university education so that all students can study for free, while others think students or their families should pay the fees. I will discuss both views, but I personally support a mixed system.

Those who support free education argue that it gives everyone an equal chance. In Bangladesh, many talented students from poor families cannot continue their studies because they cannot afford tuition, books and accommodation. If the government paid for university, these students could become doctors or engineers and help their communities. A better educated population also helps the economy, so free education can be seen as an investment. In countries such as Germany, for example, public universities charge very little, and this has helped many young people from ordinary families to graduate.

On the other hand, supporters of fees say that the government has limited money and must also spend on hospitals, roads and schools. When students pay something, they usually take their studies more seriously and do not waste time. Moreover, if there are no fees, universities may become overcrowded and lack money for good teachers and equipment, which lowers the quality of education. Graduates also earn higher salaries, so it seems fair that they pay part of the cost. Without enough money, even free universities cannot give students a good learning environment, and graduates may struggle to find jobs.

In my opinion, neither system is perfect. I think universities should charge low fees, and the government should give scholarships and cheap loans to students who cannot pay. In this way, education stays affordable and the quality can be protected.
band7.comment: Both views are covered and the opinion is clear, with relevant support, which fits Band 7. The language is correct but ordinary, and some points (quality, fairness) are stated without being fully developed.

band8.essay:
Whether higher education should be funded by taxpayers or by students is a long-running debate. Although free tuition is attractive, I believe a system of modest fees backed by generous financial support is the fairer and more sustainable option. Both positions rest on a view of who benefits from a degree, the individual or the public.

Advocates of free tuition emphasise opportunity. When fees are high, ability counts for less than family income, and bright students from rural districts of Bangladesh may abandon their ambitions before they begin. Free places also benefit society at large, since graduates in medicine, engineering and teaching supply skills that the whole country needs. Countries such as Germany have kept public universities largely free for this reason, treating them as public infrastructure much like roads. Finland and Norway follow similar models, and their graduates enter the workforce without debt, which allows them to start businesses or families earlier.

Yet there are persuasive arguments for cost-sharing. Public budgets are finite, and unrestricted free places can spread resources so thinly that classrooms become overcrowded and laboratories outdated, which damages the very quality students are promised. Because graduates typically earn considerably more than non-graduates over a lifetime, it is also arguable that those who gain most should contribute something, whereas a taxpayer who never attended university would effectively subsidise them. Finally, students who contribute financially tend to choose courses with greater care, which reduces dropout rates and wasted public funds.

On balance, I favour low fees combined with means-tested grants and income-contingent loans repaid only after graduates reach a certain salary. This protects access for the poorest students while giving universities the stable funding they need to maintain standards. Such a compromise treats education as both a public good and a personal investment.
band8.comment: Each view is presented fairly and with its strongest reasoning, and the writer's opinion grows logically out of the discussion. Precise terms (means-tested grants, income-contingent loans, cost-sharing) and varied sentence structures lift it to a high band.

structure.note: Frames the debate and signals a middle-ground opinion from the start.
Presents the equal-opportunity and public-benefit case with a comparison to Germany.
Presents the funding-limits and fairness case for cost-sharing.
Gives the writer's specific funding model and the reason it works.

vocab.m: argument that has continued for years
cost split between state and students
basic facilities provided by the state

prompt: Some people believe that protecting the environment is the responsibility of governments and large companies. Others think that individuals can make a real difference through their daily choices. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
outline: View 1: governments and companies control energy, industry and rules
View 2: individual habits add up and shape demand
Opinion: both matter, but systems must lead and individuals follow
Example: river pollution from factories versus household waste in Bangladesh

band7.essay:
Environmental damage is a global concern, and people disagree about who should take action. Some argue that governments and corporations must lead, while others believe ordinary citizens can help through their lifestyle. I will discuss both views before explaining why I think the first is more important.

Those who support the role of governments and companies have a strong argument. Factories, power plants and transport systems produce most pollution, and individuals cannot change them alone. In Bangladesh, for instance, untreated waste from tanneries and textile factories has badly polluted rivers such as the Buriganga. Only strict laws and regular inspections can stop this kind of damage. Governments can also invest in public transport and renewable energy, which gives people a greener choice that they would not have otherwise.

On the other hand, personal choices should not be dismissed. When millions of people save electricity, avoid wasting water and reduce plastic use, the total effect is large. Consumers also influence companies, because businesses will change their products if customers demand greener options. In addition, people who act responsibly at home often encourage their families and neighbours to do the same, which slowly changes social attitudes. In my opinion, governments and large companies carry the greater responsibility because they have more power and resources. A single household cannot clean a river or build a metro line. However, citizens still have an important role, because laws work better when the public supports them and follows the rules.

In conclusion, both groups are needed, but strong government action and responsible business practice should come first, with individuals supporting these efforts through their everyday behaviour.
band7.comment: Both views are discussed and a clear opinion is given, with a relevant local example. The ideas are sound but lack depth, and the vocabulary and linking are accurate yet often basic, which keeps it at Band 7.

band8.essay:
Whether environmental protection should rest with institutions or with individuals is a question that divides opinion. While personal choices have some value, I believe that governments and major companies must carry the principal burden, with citizens playing a supporting part.

The case for institutional responsibility rests on scale and control. The bulk of emissions and toxic waste originates in power generation, heavy industry and freight, sectors that no household can alter through restraint alone. The tanneries and dyeing units that discharge untreated effluent into the Buriganga River, for example, are far beyond the reach of a consumer's conscience; only enforceable standards and credible penalties can change their conduct. Governments also shape the options available to citizens, since a commuter cannot choose a cleaner bus network that has never been built.

Those who emphasise individual action make a fair point, though. Consumption patterns send signals to producers, and the cumulative effect of millions of small decisions, from cutting electricity use to refusing unnecessary packaging, is far from trivial. Personal behaviour also carries a social dimension: a family that composts or separates its rubbish may prompt neighbours to follow, gradually shifting what is considered normal in a community. On balance, I give priority to the institutional side, because individual virtue without infrastructure tends to be limited and uneven. Nevertheless, regulation depends on public consent to work, so citizens who vote, comply with rules and pressure businesses are an essential part of any lasting solution.

In short, systemic change must lead, but it is individuals who make that change politically possible and socially durable. Effective environmental policy therefore requires both, in that order of priority.
band8.comment: The response weighs each view fairly and builds a persuasive, consistent opinion, ending with a clear order of priority. Vocabulary such as 'enforceable standards' and 'cumulative effect' is precise, and complex sentences are controlled with only minimal repetition.

structure.note: Names the debate and gives the writer's opinion up front so the position is clear from the start.
Presents the institutional view with arguments about scale, control and a river pollution example.
Gives the individual-action view fairly, then states which side takes priority and why.
Reaffirms that systems lead and individuals support, ending on the order of priority.

vocab.m: rules that can be applied legally
total result from many small actions

prompt: Some people think that elderly parents should live with their adult children, while others believe that it is better for them to live in care homes. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
outline: View 1: family gives love, security, saves money
View 2: care homes give medical care when families are busy
Opinion: family home preferred, care homes as backup
Bangladesh context: joint family tradition under pressure

band7.essay:
The question of where older people should spend their final years is becoming more important as populations age. Some believe they should stay with their children, whereas others prefer care homes. I will discuss both views before explaining why I support the first.

Those who favour living with family argue that elderly people need emotional support more than anything else. In Bangladesh, it is traditional for parents to stay with their sons or daughters, and grandparents often help by looking after grandchildren and telling them stories. Being surrounded by relatives prevents loneliness, which is a major cause of depression among older people. Furthermore, this arrangement is cheaper, because the family shares one home and does not have to pay monthly fees to an institution.

On the other hand, supporters of care homes point out that adult children are often too busy to give proper attention. Both husband and wife may work long hours, and a grandmother who needs help with medicine or walking could be left alone for most of the day. In a care home, trained nurses are available all the time, and residents can make friends of their own age. For people with serious illnesses such as dementia, professional care may be safer than what a family can provide.

In my opinion, living with family is the better choice in most cases, because love and companionship cannot be replaced by paid staff. However, if the parents have complex medical needs or the family cannot cope, a good care home is a reasonable alternative. Families should make this decision together with the elderly person rather than forcing it on them.
band7.comment: Both views are discussed and the opinion is clear, with relevant examples, which meets Band 7. The ideas stay fairly predictable, the final paragraph is a little thin on development, and some word choices ('big', 'proper') are everyday rather than precise.

band8.essay:
As life expectancy rises, families must decide who will look after ageing parents. Some argue that they belong in their children's homes, while others favour residential care. Both positions have merit, but I believe the family home is preferable in most circumstances.

Advocates of multigenerational living emphasise emotional wellbeing. In Bangladesh, where respect for elders is a deeply rooted value, grandparents often occupy a central place in daily life, supervising grandchildren and passing on stories and customs. This sense of purpose protects against the isolation that frequently accompanies old age and is closely linked to depression. There is also a financial argument: sharing one household spares the family the recurring fees that quality care homes charge, which most middle-income families would struggle to afford. In addition, an older person who remains in familiar surroundings is spared the disorientation of relocating to an unfamiliar institution late in life.

Those who favour care homes counter that modern family life leaves little room for caregiving. When both spouses work long hours, an elderly parent who needs help with medication or mobility may spend most of the day alone. Residential facilities, by contrast, can offer round-the-clock nursing, supervised safety and a community of peers. For conditions such as advanced dementia, specialist attention may genuinely exceed what even devoted relatives can provide.

On balance, I side with family care, since companionship and a feeling of belonging are difficult for any institution to replicate. Nevertheless, this should not become a rigid rule. Where medical needs are complex or the household cannot cope, a well-run care home is a humane and responsible choice, provided the decision is made with the parent rather than for them.
band8.comment: The essay treats both views fairly with specific, well-chosen support and reaches a nuanced opinion that is stated from the introduction onward. Lexical range (multigenerational, residential facilities, round-the-clock) and sentence variety are strong and errors are rare.

structure.note: Introduces the dilemma, outlines both views and signals the writer's preference.
Presents the pro-family view through emotional wellbeing, cultural values and cost.
Presents the care-home view through busy households and professional medical care.
Gives a balanced personal opinion favouring family care with a clear exception.

vocab.m: belief held strongly for a long time
nursing available all day and night

prompt: Some people think that governments should control what newspapers and television channels publish. Others believe that the media should be free to report whatever it chooses. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
outline: View 1: control prevents false, harmful or hateful content
View 2: free media holds power to account
Own view: freedom with clear legal limits, not prior control
Example: misinformation, corruption reporting

band7.essay:
People have different opinions about whether governments should control the media. Some believe that official control is necessary, while others think journalists should be free. I will discuss both views before giving my own opinion.

Those who support government control argue that the media can cause serious harm if nobody supervises it. Some channels broadcast false stories or hateful messages, and this can create fear or even violence between groups. Children can also see violent or unsuitable programmes on television. If the government checks the content, it can stop dangerous material before it reaches the public, and it can protect the country in times of crisis.

However, others believe that a free media is an important part of a healthy society. Journalists often report on corruption and mistakes made by officials, and this helps citizens to know the truth. If the government controls newspapers, it may hide its own failures and publish only good news. In some countries, reporters are afraid to write about powerful people, and the public cannot trust what they read. A free press therefore protects the rights of ordinary people, and this is why many citizens value independent journalists highly.

In my opinion, the media should be mainly free, but with clear rules. Journalists who publish lies or damage someone's reputation should be punished by independent courts, not by officials who decide what can be printed in advance. This approach protects both freedom and the public. In conclusion, government control may prevent some harm, but too much control is dangerous for democracy, so I believe a free media with legal responsibility is the best solution for any country that wants an honest and informed society.
band7.comment: Both views are covered and the opinion is clear, with a logical structure. Ideas are sensible but fairly general, and the vocabulary and sentence variety stay at a safe, common level.

band8.essay:
The question of who should decide what the media publishes divides opinion. One camp sees state supervision as a safeguard for society; the other regards editorial independence as essential. I believe the second position is stronger, though not without qualification.

Advocates of control point to the real damage that irresponsible reporting can do. A fabricated story about a religious group, circulated by a television channel or a newspaper, can inflame tension within hours, and sensational coverage of crime may violate the privacy of victims or encourage imitation. Officials argue that only the state has the authority to intervene quickly enough, and that broadcasters seeking higher ratings cannot be relied upon to regulate themselves. Protecting children from graphic content is a similar and more widely accepted concern.

Yet the argument for freedom carries greater weight, because the media's most valuable function is scrutiny of power. Investigations into bribery in public contracts or unsafe factories, as occurred after the Rana Plaza collapse, depend on reporters who are not answerable to the very people they examine. Once a government approves content in advance, it gains an obvious incentive to suppress unfavourable news, and self-censorship soon follows as editors avoid topics that might provoke officials. The public then loses the information it needs to judge its leaders.

My view is that the media should operate without prior approval but within laws on defamation, incitement and privacy, enforced by independent courts and a transparent complaints body. This preserves the watchdog role while giving those harmed by false reporting a means of redress. In conclusion, state control is a blunt instrument that tends to protect governments rather than citizens. Freedom accompanied by legal accountability is the more reliable way to serve the public interest.
band8.comment: Both sides are presented fairly, then the writer's view is argued with a specific mechanism (prior approval leading to self-censorship). The essay uses a precise range of vocabulary, a relevant real example and a nuanced, balanced conclusion.

structure.note: Frames the debate and signals a preference with a qualification.
Presents the pro-control case fairly, with a concrete risk and a child-protection point.
Argues for freedom through the watchdog role and self-censorship, then gives the writer's own legal model.
Concludes that accountable freedom serves the public better than control.

vocab.m: freedom of editors from outside pressure
close checking of those in authority
a way to get justice or compensation

prompt: Some people believe that automation and robots will destroy many jobs, while others think that technology will create new kinds of work. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
outline: View 1: machines are cheaper and faster, so low-skilled workers lose jobs (garment factories)
View 2: new jobs appear in programming, maintenance and freelancing
Opinion: both happen; the key issue is retraining

band7.essay:
Some people believe that automation and robots will destroy many jobs, whereas others think technology will create new kinds of work. I will discuss both views before giving my opinion.

Those who fear job losses have a strong point. Machines can work faster than humans, do not need rest, and do not ask for a salary. Many garment factories in Bangladesh, for example, have started to use automatic cutting and sewing machines, and this means fewer workers are needed. Workers with little education are affected most, and they may find it hard to get another job quickly. The owners of factories like automation because it reduces costs, but ordinary workers may lose the income that supports their whole family.

However, history shows that new technology also creates jobs. When computers became popular, new jobs appeared for programmers, designers and technicians who repair machines. In the same way, robots need people to build, program and maintain them. Furthermore, cheaper production can make companies grow and employ more people in other departments such as sales and delivery. The freelancing industry in Bangladesh is a good example, because many young people now earn money from online work which did not exist twenty years ago. In addition, e-commerce has created thousands of delivery and warehouse jobs, which shows that technology can open new opportunities for people with different levels of education.

In my opinion, automation will remove some jobs but create others, so the real problem is training. Governments and companies should provide skills courses for workers so that they can move into the new jobs, and then technology can benefit society.
band7.comment: The essay discusses both sides and gives a clear opinion with local examples, which supports Band 7. Vocabulary is mostly general and the argument for each side is fairly short, with little analysis of why the transition is difficult.

band8.essay:
Predictions about automation tend to swing between utopia and mass unemployment. In my view, technology will indeed displace many existing roles, but it is likely to generate enough new ones, provided workers are given the means to adapt.

The pessimistic case deserves to be taken seriously. Machines now perform repetitive tasks more cheaply and consistently than people, and the effects are visible in manufacturing. As Bangladesh's ready-made garment sector installs automated cutting and sewing equipment, thousands of semi-skilled workers, many of them women, face the prospect of redundancy. Because these workers have limited formal education, retraining is difficult, and the transition can be painful for entire communities. In addition, the pace of change leaves little time to adjust, since a factory can install machines in months while a worker may need years to acquire new skills.

Nonetheless, the optimists can point to a long record in which technology has created more work than it destroyed. The spread of the internet eliminated many clerical posts yet gave rise to software development, digital marketing and logistics, and freelancing now earns Bangladesh substantial foreign currency. Automation also lowers production costs, which can stimulate demand and prompt firms to expand, hiring in areas such as design, maintenance and customer service that machines cannot easily replicate. Previous waves of mechanisation, from the printing press to the personal computer, inspired similar fears yet ultimately widened employment.

Ultimately, the outcome depends less on the machines than on policy. If governments and employers invest in vocational retraining and support workers through the transition, automation can raise productivity without leaving a generation behind. Societies that plan for this transition tend to emerge with higher productivity and wages.
band8.comment: The discussion is balanced and analytical: it explains why displacement hurts (limited education makes retraining hard) and why job creation occurs (lower costs stimulate demand). The opinion is conditional and mature, and phrases like displace existing roles and vocational retraining are precise.

structure.note: Sets up the debate and states a conditional opinion.
Develops the job-loss view with the garment sector and the retraining barrier.
Develops the job-creation view with historical precedent and demand effects.
Shifts the focus from machines to retraining policy.

vocab.m: loss of a job as no longer needed

prompt: Some people think that mental health should receive the same attention and funding as physical health. Others believe that physical illnesses should be a higher priority. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
outline: View 1: physical illness is visible, measurable and often life-threatening
View 2: mental illness affects work, family and can lead to suicide
Opinion: equal priority because the two are linked
Bangladesh context: stigma and very few psychiatrists

band7.essay:
Health systems have limited budgets, so governments must decide where to spend money. Some people believe that physical diseases should come first, while others argue that mental health deserves equal attention. Although I understand the first view, I agree more with the second.

Those who prioritise physical health point out that diseases such as cancer, tuberculosis and dengue are visible and can kill quickly. In a developing country like Bangladesh, many people still lack basic hospital services, clean water and vaccines. It is therefore understandable that the government spends most of its health budget on these needs. Physical illness is also easier to diagnose and measure, so officials can see clearly whether their money has produced results.

However, mental health problems are just as serious, and they are often ignored. Conditions such as depression and anxiety can stop people from working, damage family relationships and, in the worst cases, lead to suicide. Because of social stigma, many patients in Bangladesh never see a doctor, and there are very few psychiatrists for a population of over 170 million. Students facing exam pressure and workers facing job insecurity are especially at risk, but they rarely receive help. In my opinion, mental and physical health should receive equal attention, because they are closely connected. A person with long-term depression may neglect their diet and medical care, and someone with a chronic illness often becomes anxious or sad. Treating only one side of the problem is rarely successful.

To conclude, physical health is undeniably important, but mental health deserves the same level of attention and funding. Doing this would improve both individual wellbeing and the whole economy.
band7.comment: Both views are covered, the opinion is clear and the Bangladesh context adds relevance. Ideas are mostly general, and phrasing such as 'very serious' and 'rarely successful' is less precise than Band 8 writing.

band8.essay:
Governments have finite health budgets, and the question of whether psychological wellbeing deserves parity with physical medicine is therefore a practical as well as a moral one. I acknowledge the case for putting physical illness first, but I believe the two should be treated as equally important.

Supporters of the traditional priority make a reasonable argument. Infectious diseases and cancers kill quickly and visibly, and in a country such as Bangladesh, where basic services like maternal care, clean water and immunisation remain incomplete in many districts, spending on tangible needs seems more urgent. Physical conditions are also easier to diagnose and track, which allows officials to demonstrate that public money has delivered measurable gains.

Even so, this reasoning understates the damage caused by untreated mental illness. Depression and anxiety erode productivity, strain families and, in severe cases, end in suicide. The problem is compounded by stigma, which deters many Bangladeshis from seeking help, and by a shortage of specialists that leaves millions with no realistic route to treatment. Students under intense exam pressure and workers in insecure jobs are particularly exposed, yet they are seldom identified until a crisis occurs. My own view is that the distinction between the two categories is partly artificial. Chronic stress raises the risk of heart disease, while a person with long-term illness often develops depression, so neglecting either one undermines outcomes in the other. Integrating counselling into ordinary clinics would be a cost-effective way to recognise this connection.

In conclusion, physical health will always demand substantial funding, but mental health should no longer be treated as an optional extra. Giving it equal weight would improve individual lives and strengthen the workforce on which economic progress depends.
band8.comment: The essay acknowledges the opposing side with specific reasoning, then argues that the divide is partly artificial, which gives the opinion real depth. Language is precise and varied ('erode productivity', 'compounded by stigma') and cohesion is smooth without mechanical linkers.

structure.note: Frames the budget dilemma and signals a balanced yet definite opinion.
Presents the physical-first view fairly, with Bangladesh service gaps and measurability.
Rebuts through the harms of untreated mental illness and stigma, then argues the two types of health are linked.
Restates equal priority and links it to wider benefits for society and the economy.

prompt: Some people prefer to work for a large, well-known company, while others prefer to start or join a small business. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
outline: Large company: stable salary, benefits, training, reputation
Small business: more responsibility, faster growth, flexibility
Opinion: small firm better early, large firm for security
Link to young graduates in Bangladesh

band7.essay:
Choosing a career path is an important decision, and people often disagree about whether a large corporation or a small business is the better place to work. In this essay, I will look at both options and then give my own view.

Working for a large, famous company has several benefits. First, such organisations usually offer a stable income and extra benefits like health insurance, bonuses and paid leave. This is attractive in Bangladesh, where many families depend on one salary. Second, big companies often provide formal training programmes, so employees can improve their skills and move up gradually. Having a respected name on a CV can also help a person find a better job in the future.

However, a small business has its own attractions. In a small team, each person is given more responsibility, and a young employee may handle tasks that would take years to reach in a large firm. Decisions are made quickly, which allows workers to see the results of their ideas. Those who start their own business can also be their own boss and earn a higher income if the business succeeds. On the other hand, small firms are risky, since many of them close within a few years and salaries may not be paid on time.

In my opinion, the best choice depends on a person's stage of life. Fresh graduates can learn very fast in a small company because they have to do many different jobs, and the risk is lower when they have no family to support. Later, when they need security, a large company is probably more suitable. Therefore, I think both options are useful at different times.
band7.comment: Both views and an opinion are present and the essay is easy to follow, so it reaches Band 7. Support is accurate but quite general, linking words are repetitive ('However', 'On the other hand'), and the vocabulary lacks the precision of higher bands.

band8.essay:
Graduates today face a genuine choice between the security of a corporation and the freedom of a small enterprise. Each route has distinct strengths, but I believe the better option depends largely on the stage of one's career.

The appeal of large companies lies chiefly in stability. They typically offer predictable salaries, health cover and paid leave, which matters greatly in Bangladesh, where one income often supports an extended family. They also invest in structured training and clear promotion ladders, so employees can build expertise methodically. Furthermore, a recognised brand on a résumé acts as a credential, opening doors in later job applications. Large employers also tend to comply with labour regulations, so overtime, leave and pension entitlements are less likely to be ignored.

Small businesses, however, offer a different kind of reward. With a lean team, even a junior employee may manage clients, solve problems and see the impact of a decision within days, whereas the same responsibility might take years to earn in a bureaucratic organisation. Entrepreneurs also stand to keep the profits of their own efforts, and the independence of running a business suits people who dislike following rigid procedures. The trade-off is risk: many start-ups fail within a few years, and payment can be irregular when cash flow is tight.

Weighing these factors, I would recommend that young people begin in a small firm, where the learning curve is steepest and the personal cost of failure is lowest because they usually have few dependants. Once they have family obligations, the predictability of a large employer becomes more valuable. Rather than treating the choice as permanent, workers can regard each type of employer as suited to a particular phase of working life.
band8.comment: The discussion is balanced and the writer's opinion is both clear and argued rather than asserted. Vocabulary is natural and precise (credential, lean team, cash flow, learning curve), and the sentence structures are varied and controlled.

structure.note: Sets up the choice and states that the answer depends on career stage.
Explains why large companies attract people: stability, training and reputation.
Explains small-business benefits of responsibility and ownership, with the risk trade-off.
Offers an opinion that matches the employer type to life stage.

vocab.m: clear steps for moving up in a company
money coming in is barely enough
most new skills are learned quickly
few people relying on your income

prompt: Some people believe that tourism is very good for local communities. Others think it damages the traditional culture and natural environment of the places visited. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
outline: View 1: jobs, income, infrastructure
View 2: commercialised culture, pollution, rising prices
Own view: benefits greater if tourism is managed
Example: Cox's Bazar or Sundarbans

band7.essay:
Tourism is an important industry in many countries today. Some people think it helps local communities, while others believe it causes damage to culture and nature. I will discuss both views and explain why I take a middle position.

Supporters of tourism say that it brings many economic benefits. Hotels, restaurants and transport companies employ local people, and small sellers can earn money by selling food and handicrafts to visitors. In Cox's Bazar, for example, thousands of families depend on the money that tourists spend. The income from tourism can also pay for better roads, electricity and airports, which improve daily life for residents as well as visitors.

On the other hand, critics point out several problems. When too many tourists arrive, beaches and forests can become dirty and crowded, and wildlife may be disturbed or driven away. Traditional culture can also suffer, because local dances and ceremonies are sometimes changed to entertain visitors and lose their real meaning. In addition, prices of land and food often rise, so local people may find it difficult to live in their own towns.

In my opinion, tourism can be very useful for local communities, but only when it is managed carefully. The government should limit the number of visitors in sensitive places, make hotels follow environmental rules and make sure that local people receive a fair share of the profits. Visitors should also be educated to respect local customs. In conclusion, tourism has both benefits and risks, and with good planning, I believe the advantages can be much greater than the disadvantages for everyone involved.
band7.comment: The essay covers both views and gives a clear opinion with an example. It is well organised, but support is fairly generic and the language is correct rather than precise or varied.

band8.essay:
Opinion is divided on whether tourism enriches or erodes the communities that host it. Both claims contain truth, but I believe the outcome depends largely on how the industry is governed.

The economic case is persuasive. Tourism creates work for people with limited formal education, from boatmen and guides to hotel staff and street vendors, and the spending of visitors circulates through the local economy rather than leaving it. On the Cox's Bazar coast, entire neighbourhoods rely on seasonal arrivals. Revenue can also fund infrastructure that residents would not otherwise receive, and a financial interest in preserving attractions gives communities a practical reason to protect forests, reefs and historic buildings.

The opposing view is nonetheless serious. Heavy visitor numbers strain fragile ecosystems: waste accumulates on beaches, boat traffic disturbs wildlife, and hotels built too close to the shore accelerate erosion. Culture can be reduced to a commodity when ceremonies are shortened or altered to suit a tourist timetable, leaving performers detached from the traditions they represent. Rising land values may also push out the very residents whose way of life attracted visitors, while the largest profits often go to outside investors or tour operators.

Taking both sides into account, I consider tourism a net benefit when regulated sensibly. Authorities should cap numbers at ecologically sensitive sites such as the Sundarbans, require waste management from hotel owners, and encourage community-run lodges and guiding so that income stays local. Visitor education about dress and behaviour would also reduce friction. In conclusion, tourism is neither a guaranteed blessing nor an inevitable harm. Where planning protects the environment and shares the proceeds fairly, communities gain far more than they lose.
band8.comment: Both views are developed with specific effects (erosion, culture as commodity, profits leaving the area). The writer offers a justified, practical position, and the language is varied and accurate with strong collocations.

structure.note: Introduces the debate and signals that governance decides the outcome.
Develops the economic and conservation incentives with a local example.
Explains ecological strain, cultural commodification and outside profit.
Gives a managed-tourism recommendation and closes with a balanced conclusion.

vocab.m: money keeps moving among local businesses
something treated only as a product to sell

prompt: In many countries, a large number of school students attend private coaching classes in addition to their regular lessons. What problems can this cause, and what can be done to reduce the need for private coaching?
outline: Problems: tired students with no free time; high cost and inequality
Problems: teachers who tutor their own pupils
Solutions: better teacher pay and training; ban tutoring own pupils
Solutions: free remedial classes and exam reform

band7.essay:
In many countries, including Bangladesh, school students attend private coaching classes after their normal lessons. This causes several problems for students and families, but there are some solutions that schools and governments can use.

The first problem is that students become very tired and have little free time. They go to school in the morning and then to coaching in the afternoon and evening, so they cannot play sports, rest or spend time with their family. This can also affect their health and increase stress. Another problem is the cost. Poor families may spend a large part of their income on coaching fees, and children who cannot pay are at a disadvantage compared with richer students, which makes education unequal. As a result, some students lose interest in their school lessons because they have already studied the topics outside.

To solve these problems, the first solution is to improve the quality of teaching in schools. If teachers are well trained and paid a better salary, they will explain the lessons clearly, and parents will not feel that extra classes are necessary.
